title_content.content: Exploration of poly(1,4‑butanediol diglycidyl ether, 2‑methylimidazole, and imidazole) as leveling agents in blind hole copper plating

paragraph_content.content: Xiangjian Zeng<sup>1</sup>, Zhanchang Pan<sup>1,</sup>* , Guanghui Hu<sup>1</sup>, Guowei Xia<sup>2</sup>, Haiqing Huang<sup>2</sup>, Mingliang Zou<sup>2</sup>, and Shikun Shi<sup>2</sup>

Literature reports indicate that existing synthesis methods for leveling agents often sufer from complex procedures, high environmental burden, challenging purification processes, and insuficient via filling eficiency. To address these limitations, a novel leveling agent (CDT) was synthesized using environmentally friendly materials through a simplified, cost-efective process that eliminates the need for post-synthesis purification. This study systematically investigates the influence of CDT on blind via filling performance in an acidic copper sulfate plating bath containing polyethylene glycol (PEG), bis(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS), and chloride ions. The chemical structure of CDT was characterized by Fouriertransform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), and gel permeation chromatography (GPC). Quantum chemical calculations and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations revealed that CDT exhibits stronger adsorption on copper surfaces compared to conventional leveling agents. Electrochemical measurements confirmed its ability to suppress copper deposition and helped determine the optimal working concentration of CDT. Electroplating experiments further demonstrated CDT’s capability to achieve superfilling, indicating its suitability for printed circuit board (PCB) manufacturing. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) results corroborated the validity of the optimal concentration established by electrochemical tests. Finally, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) confirmed strong interfacial interactions between CDT and the copper surface. These findings collectively suggest that CDT is a highly promising candidate for advanced leveling agent applications.

Printed Circuit Boards (PCBs) are indispensable components in modern daily life. As current electronic devices trend toward lighter, thinner, and smaller designs, PCB technology is correspondingly evolving toward multi-layer and high-density configurations. In the PCB manufacturing industry, blind via technology plays a crucial role as it facilitates conductive connections between the layers of multi-layer circuit boards. Therefore, the metallization technology for blind vias is particularly critical in this rapidly advancing field [1–4].

To meet the high-performance demands of current electronic devices, copper electroplating in blind vias must achieve flawless filling without cracks and gaps. This typically involves superfilling or botom-up filling techniques, where superfilling refers to a deposition process during electroplating in which the copper deposition rate at the botom of the blind vias is significantly higher than at the opening and surface, thereby achieving perfect filling of the vias [5]. To accomplish superfilling, an acidic copper sulfate system is com monly used in industrial applications. In this system, the choice of additives is crucial, primarily including accelerators, suppressors, and leveling agents. Accelerators, usually sulfur-containing organic compounds, adsorb on the electrode surface, refine the copper crystal structure, and promote copper nucleation. Their primary function is to combine with chloride ions to achieve depolarization, thus increasing the cathodic current density [6–9]. The most widely studied and used accelerators include SPS and MPS [10, 11]. Sup pressors, such as polyether polymers (e.g., PEG and PPG) [12–14], mainly inhibit the deposition of copper during electroplating by adsorbing on the surface of the plated parts and preventing the difusion of
{ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }

[15–17]. In systems containing both accelerators and suppressors, the role of leveling agents is indispensable. Leveling agents typically include certain nitrogencontaining organic compounds [18, 19], such as the dye-type leveling agents JGB [20], DB [18], ABPV [21, 22], and heterocyclic non-dye leveling agents such as 2-amino-4-methylbenzothiazole [23] (AMBT) and 2-mercaptopyridine [24, 25] (2-MP). Their main func tion is to work synergistically with suppressors to inhibit copper deposition on the surface of the plated parts, optimize current density distribution, enhance filling eficiency, and thereby prevent premature hole sealing that leads to voids [25–30]. Although the most efective leveling agents are often commercial secrets, high costs and poor environmental friendliness in the market make the development of new leveling agents both time-consuming and labor-intensive. Consequently, to date, only a few superfilling leveling agents have been specifically reported [31–33].

The importance of leveling agents in superfilling copper electroplating has been corroborated by numerous researchers. Literatures [34, 35] frequently mention Janus Green B (JGB) as an efective leveling agent that not only enhances the fill rate of blind vias but also reduces the issue of protrusions during filling. Myung Hyun Lee and other researchers [36] synthesized a leveling agent containing two quaternary ammonium groups and hexaglycerol, which successfully achieved seamless and void-free filling of blind vias. Xu and colleagues [29] designed and synthesized quaternary ammonium salts of diketopyrrolopyrrole (DPP) with various aryl substituents. Additionally, Kim and others [37] developed a choline-based leveling agent, 1,5-bis(2-N,N,Ntrimethylaminoethyl) pentanedioate diiodide, used as a modulator in copper electroplating solutions. Meanwhile, TCA [23] and DMP [38] have also been reported as potential leveling agents. Their synthesis processes are complex, the purification is challenging, and the raw material costs are high, all factors that are unfavorable for industrial production.

This study, based on a comprehensive analysis of existing literature, aims to develop a novel superfilling leveling agent. During the synthesis process, dimethylimidazole, imidazole, and 1,4-butanediol diglycidyl ether were selected as raw materials, and a detailed characterization of the organic structure of the resulting leveling agent was performed. By integrating quantum chemical calculations and molecular dynamics simulations, this research thoroughly analyzed active sites and adsorption behaviors to elucidate the interaction mechanisms between the organic molecules and the copper surface. Furthermore, the filling mechanism of the leveling agent was investigated using theoretical calculations, electrochemical measurements, and techniques such as Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) and X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS). Additionally, electroplating experiments were conducted to validate the filling eficacy of the leveling agent and confirm its suitability for specific requirements in Printed Circuit Board (PCB) applications.

The employed testing methods included cyclic voltammetry (CV), linear sweep voltammetry (LSV), and galvanostatic measurement (GM). In this study, field emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM, model S-3400N) was utilized to conduct detailed scanning electron microscopy (SEM) analysis of the copper surface morphologies under different electroplating solution conditions. To ensure accurate observation of surface morphologies, a dilute sulfuric acid solution was used to remove the oxide layer from the copper surface prior to the experiments.

To further investigate the interactions between copper samples and CDT, this study involved immersing copper samples in a solution containing CDT to observe potential chemical reactions between the copper surface and CDT. Quantum chemical calculations are a crucial method for revealing the correlation between molecular structure and inhibition efects [40]. To understand the inhibitory action of CDT, quantum chemical calculations were performed to obtain electronic properties and orbital information of the molecule, predicting active sites and elucidating adsorption mechanisms related to molecular structure. Using Gaussian software, quantum chemical calculations not only optimized the molecular structure of CDT but also calculated a series of properties such as the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO), the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO), the energy gap

paragraph_content.content: Molecular electrostatic potential (ESP) is a useful tool for visualizing reactive sites and predicting certain molecular properties [42, 43]. In ESP map, regions of positive electrostatic potential are represented in red, indicating areas of high electron density, while regions of negative potential are shown in blue, corresponding to areas of low electron density. Additionally, the red regions are associated with nucleophilic reactions, and the blue regions with electrophilic reactions [44]. As shown in Fig. 7, the red and pinkwhite areas are primarily distributed near the nitrogen atoms, while the blue areas are mainly around the carbon atoms. The ESP histogram indicates that

To further understand the role of additives in the electroplating process, molecular dynamics simulations were utilized to provide valuable insights. Using Materials Studio software, molecular dynamics simulations were conducted to explore the adsorption of leveling agent molecules on the Cu(111) crystal surface. The Cu(111) surface was selected for molecular dynamics simulation because it is the most stable, low Miller index copper surface and the most prevalent surface. Additionally, the symmetric Cu(111) surface offers advantages for systematically exploring the potential energy surface of the adsorption system [46–48].

Further calculations were performed to determine the adsorption energy of CDT on the Cu(111) substrate, as shown in Fig. 8. The imidazole rings and oxygen atoms of CDT are positioned close to the copper surface, like the case with VIBDGE. Calculated using the formula, the
E _ { \mathrm { A d s o r p t i o n } }

of CDT reached − 2.125 eV, indicating a strong afinity of CDT’s imidazole rings for the Cu surface. According to molecular dynamics results, CDT exhibits excellent inhibitory performance on copper deposition. Moreover, the linear structure of CDT allows for more efective spatial coverage on the copper surface [49].

Based on theoretical calculations, CDT is identified as a potential leveling agent. Thus, electrochemical tests were conducted to further validate its efects, starting with cyclic voltammetry to study the impact of various concentrations of CDT on copper deposition, with results shown in Fig. 9a–b. As observed from Fig. 9, the dissolution peak of copper is highest without any additives. The addition of 200 mg/L PEG and 1 mg/L SPS significantly reduces the copper dissolution peak due to the inhibitory action of PEG-Cl<sup>−</sup>. The introduction of the leveling agent CDT further decreases the copper dissolution peak, indicating that the addition of CDT enhances cathodic polarization and inhibits copper deposition. To compare the efects of diferent additives on the dissolution peaks of copper, the dissolution peaks at diferent CDT concentrations were quantitatively calculated using cyclic voltammetry, with average values from three parallel experiments presented in Table 2. It is evident that in the base plating solution without additives, the area of the copper dissolution peak is the largest, regardless of the rotation speed. The area of the CVS peak at 1000 rpm is greater than that at 100 rpm, indicating that the additive-free electrolyte cannot efectively inhibit the formation of copper deposition on the micro-pore surface, thus failing to achieve micro-pore filling. After adding 200 mg/L PEG, 1 mg/L SPS, and various concentrations of CDT, the CVS peak area at 1000 rpm is significantly smaller than at 100 rpm, indicating the inhibitory efect of CDT under strong convection cathodic reduction, and the relationship between copper dissolution peaks and CDT concentration is not linear. Linear sweep voltammetry was further employed to analyze the role of CDT within the electrolyte, as depicted in Fig. 9(c-d). The graph illustrates that the addition of additives significantly influences copper deposition. Relative to the base plating solution without additives, the inclusion of SPS and PEG in the electrolyte solution results in a negative shift of the reduction potential. Studies indicate that the inhibitory efect of PEG on copper deposition is due to the adsorption layer of PEG at the cathode interface, which impedes the reduction process of copper ions facilitated by Cl<sup>−</sup> [50, 51]. With SPS and PEG present in the electrolyte, the introduction of CDT further enhances cathodic polarization behavior. After adding the additives, the cathodic potential at 1000 rpm is more polarized than at 100 rpm, demonstrating that the additives exert a stronger inhibitory efect on copper deposition in areas of strong convection. Upon adding 1 mg/L of CDT, the initial potential of copper begins to shift negatively. As the concentration of CDT increases, this negative shift in the starting potential becomes more pronounced, indicating that CDT can enhance cathodic polarization by adsorbing onto the copper surface, thus inhibiting copper deposition. This change is consistent with the trends observed in the cathodic peak areas in Fig. 9a and b. Cathodic polarization increases with CDT concentration, as higher concentrations lead to more adsorption on the cathode surface, thereby providing stronger inhibition of cathodic copper ion reduction. When the concentration of CDT reaches
5 \ \mathrm { m g / L } ,

changes in the copper deposition potential become less distinct, like that seen at 6 mg/L, suggesting that saturation inhibition is essentially achieved at 5 mg/L. Thus, the optimal concentration of CDT is confirmed to be 5 mg/L, consistent with results from cyclic voltammetry.

paragraph_content.content: Based on the research and analysis presented, it can be inferred that CDT can serve as a leveling agent for micro-via filling in PCBs. To evaluate the filling efficacy of CDT as a leveling agent, electroplating experiments were conducted at various concentrations of CDT and compared with a commercial JGB formulation. Figure 11 shows the cross-sectional optical microscopy images of the micro-vias after electroplating. As depicted in Fig. 11a, without the addition of a leveling agent, a significant void is observed at the botom of the via, resulting from uneven current density due to varying convection intensities. With the injection of 1 mg/L CDT, the filling performance of the micro-vias notably improves. As illustrated in Figs. 11b–f, the optimal micro-via filling performance occurs at a CDT concentration of 5 mg/L, consistent with the previous electrochemical testing results. When the CDT concentration is increased to 6 mg/L, the filling rate decreases, and the performance deteriorates, indicating that there is a specific operational concentration range for the leveling agent. If the concentration is too low, the inhibitory efect is insuficient, leading to void formation. Conversely, if the concen tration is too high, it disrupts the balance among the additives, resulting in poor filling performance. The JGB electroplating formula, commonly used in the industry, serves as a benchmark for comparing the filling performance of newly discovered leveling agents. Figure 11h shows the filling efect using the commercial JGB electroplating solution, which is inferior to the efect achieved with 5 mg/L CDT. The JGB formula results in some concavity and does not completely fill the blind vias, whereas CDT achieves superfilling of micro-vias, demonstrating its potential as an efective leveling agent.

The influence of different concentrations of CDT on the surface morphology of copper is depicted in Fig. 12. In the absence of CDT in the plating solution, the copper plating surface exhibits a rough, blocky, and distinctly porous appearance. Conversely, compared to the CDT-free condition, the addition of varying concentrations of CDT to the plating solution significantly improves the surface morphology of the copper plating (Figs. 12b–h). The formation of smooth planes is due to the modification of the plating layer after adding CDT, which initiates crystal refinement. However, when the CDT concentration is increased to 5 mg/L, a proliferation of small blocky crystals appears on the copper surface, becoming denser with increasing concentrations of CDT. These results indicate that CDT demonstrates its leveling capability efectively within a certain concentration range, but as the concentration of the leveling agent increases, the synergistic interactions among the additives are disrupted. Similar results have been reported in copper electrodepositing studies [18, 21].

While molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and XPS ofer diferent perspectives—thermodynamic interaction versus chemical bonding—they provide complementary evidence supporting the strong adsorption of CDT on the copper surface. Figure 13a displays the X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) full spectrum of a copper sample after soaking for 40 min in an electroplating solution containing CDT. This full spectrum, obtained through detailed scanning, reveals the presence of carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, sulfur, and copper on the copper surface, confirming the adsorption of CDT. Detailed spectra for Cu2p3/2, C1s, and N1s can be found in Figs. 13b–d. In Fig. 13b, the chemi cal states on the copper surface are shown by the peaks of Cu2p3/2 and Cu2p1/2, located at binding energies of 931.8 and 951.6 eV, respectively. The Cu2p3/2 peak in Fig. 13b can be further divided into subpeaks for Cu<sub>2</sub>O (931.8 eV) and CuO (933.7 eV) [58], indicating the formation of a copper oxide layer on the copper surface due to oxidation in air and reaction with water molecules in the solution, predominantly in the form of Cu O [59]. Figure 13c focuses on the N1s spectrum, displaying two peaks at 397.8 eV (C–N or C=N) and 399.2 eV (Cu–N), which deviate slightly from the nitrogen binding energies reported in previous literature, suggesting the possible formation of structures such as Cu–N–C or Cu–N=C on the CDT-modified copper surface [60–62]. The C1s spectrum (seen in Fig. 13d) reveals six diferent peaks corresponding to 283.66 eV (C=C), 284.03 eV (C–C), 284.42 eV (C–H), 284.92 eV (C–N), 285.9 eV (C–O), and 287.63 eV (C=O) [63–65]. The presence of these peaks indicates a rich variety of carbon environments within the CDT molecule, such as double bonds between carbons, single bonds, combinations of carbon with hydrogen, and carbon with nitrogen, providing crucial clues for understanding how CDT achieves adsorption on the copper surface.

paragraph_content.content: In summary, we have selected the nitrogen-heterocyclic compound CDT as an electroplating leveling agent for copper micro-via filling. The synthesis of CDT was successfully confirmed by infrared, hydrogen nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, and gel permeation chromatography results. Quantum chemical simulations suggest that CDT possesses the potential to occupy metal vacant orbitals for adsorption. Moreover, molecular dynamics simulations indicate that CDT exhibits strong affinity for copper surfaces. Electrochemical tests revealed that the optimal working concentration of CDT is 5 mg/L. Chronopotentiometric measurements further demonstrated that CDT can synergistically suppress copper deposition when combined with other additives, exhibiting a potential diference as high as 20 mV, which indicates its strong inhibitory efect on copper electrodeposition. Electroplating tests show that the best plating results occur at a concentration of 5 mg/L, consistent with electrochemical findings. Field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) results showed that CDT can refine copper grain structures within an appropriate concentration range; however, when the concentration exceeds the optimal level, crystal agglomeration reoccurs. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) confirmed the efective adsorption of CDT on the copper surface, and the strong interaction between them provides a foundation for the suppression of copper deposition. Collectively, our research conclusively proves that CDT is a promising leveling agent for copper micro-via filling, providing theoretical guidance for the discovery and improvement of electroplating technologies for micro-via filling.
